shots.title:
When AI becomes
the research team
lines: What changes when AI starts doing the research that builds the next generation of AI?
The important shift is a feedback loop: better systems can help produce better successors, which can then accelerate the work again.

shots.title: Two numbers. Two different measures.
lines: The evidence already shows substantial automation, but the numbers need care.
The paper cites Anthropic reporting that AI wrote more than eighty percent of approved code by May twenty twenty-six.
Separately, twenty-six percent of research and development work was completed autonomously, with high-level human supervision, by August.
Writing code and owning a research workflow are different measures.

shots.title: Research is more than code.
lines: A research cycle needs an idea, an implementation, an experiment, and a judgment about the result.
Making the implementation faster helps. But an idea still has to survive testing, and somebody has to decide whether the apparent improvement is real.

shots.title: The output becomes an input.
lines: Now close the loop. A stronger model helps run that research cycle.
If the cycle produces a more capable or more efficient successor, that successor can join the research team.
The team may then do more useful work on the same hardware. That is the mechanism behind a possible software-driven intelligence explosion.

shots.title: Can the gains outrun the friction?
lines: The key question is whether expanding research capacity can overcome diminishing returns.
The paper calls this balance returns to research effort, represented by r.
In its simplified model, values above one support acceleration while that condition holds. This is an assumption to investigate, not a universal law.

shots.title: A scenario, not a countdown.
lines: One calculation suggests a tenfold increase in the pace of progress within about one and a half years after full automation.
That result assumes research returns stay at the estimated levels and no other bottlenecks emerge.
It is not a prediction that a tenfold speedup will arrive eighteen months from today.

shots.title: Four forces can slow the loop.
lines: There are four broad sources of friction: diminishing returns, limits on experimental compute and data, tasks that remain hard to automate, and processes that simply take time.
A thousand proposed experiments are not a thousand validated discoveries.
More agents cannot, by themselves, make a long training run finish instantly.

shots.title: Benefits and risks can arrive together.
lines: Faster research could bring useful scientific and medical advances closer.
But the same acceleration can leave less time to evaluate systems, preserve human control, and adapt institutions.
The paper also warns that concentrating research capability could weaken checks on power.

shots.title: Keep oversight inside the loop.
lines: Consider a research loop with an explicit checkpoint before each successor is deployed.
The checkpoint asks what improved, what failed, and whether the evidence justifies expanding access.
If generating the next model becomes fast, these checks become more consequential, not optional overhead.

shots.title: Measure. Constrain. Prepare.
lines: The authors propose three priorities: clearer reporting on research automation, ways to steer or pause risky development, and preparation for wider impacts.
The practical takeaway is to track the whole loop: useful research output, the bottlenecks that remain, and whether people can still understand and control what happens next.
